opus-5.5.text:
I think annotations are really at the heart of turning a pre-trained model into something useful. Pre-training gives you a model that has compressed a huge amount of knowledge from the web, but it doesn't know how to behave. It will just continue text. To make it follow instructions, you need to show it, through demonstrations and through preferences, what a good answer looks like.

So there are roughly two phases. First, supervised fine-tuning, where you have high-quality examples of instructions and the responses you'd want. The quality matters much more than the quantity there. A few tens of thousands of really good examples can go a long way, whereas a lot of noisy data can hurt. Then you have the preference part, where annotators compare outputs and tell you which one is better, and you use that signal to further align the model. That's often easier for humans to do than writing perfect answers from scratch, because judging is easier than producing.

What we've seen is that the bottleneck increasingly becomes the expertise of the annotators. For simple conversational tasks, generalists are fine. But as models get better, if you want them to reason well on math, code, legal questions, or domain-specific enterprise tasks, you need experts who can actually tell whether an answer is correct. And that's expensive and slow, so a lot of the work now is about being clever: using the model itself to generate candidates, having humans focus on the hard or ambiguous cases, and using automatic verification wherever you can, like running code or checking math.

The other thing I'd say is that annotation is also where a lot of the product decisions live. How verbose should the model be, when should it refuse, how should it handle ambiguity, what tone should it have. Those aren't purely technical choices, and for us it's also important that our customers can bring their own data and their own preferences to fine-tune the model for their use case. Instruction following isn't a single universal target; it depends on who's using the model and for what.

r001.rationale: The response says models can generate candidate outputs for human review, but it does not identify machine-produced annotations as a source of supervision for instruction-following training.

fable-5.1.text:
Annotations are really the bridge between a model that knows things and a model that does what you ask. When you pretrain on the web, you get a very capable compressor of human knowledge, but it has no notion of a user, of a request, of a turn. It just continues text. So the instruction-following behavior has to come from somewhere, and that somewhere is a relatively small amount of very high quality annotated data.

What surprised us, and I think surprised a lot of people, is how little you actually need. We're talking about tens of thousands of examples, not millions, if they're good. The pretrained model already has the capability latent inside it. The annotations are mostly teaching it the format of the interaction and the kind of behavior you want: be helpful, be concise, answer the actual question, don't make things up when you're unsure. You're not teaching it new knowledge, you're teaching it a role.

The quality matters much more than the quantity. One bad annotation, something that's lazy or wrong or verbose, can be quite damaging because the model takes it as a signal about what good looks like. So we invest a lot in who does the annotation and how. It's not a crowd-sourcing problem, it's closer to hiring good writers and good domain experts and giving them very precise guidelines.

Then there's the second layer, which is preference data. Instead of writing the answer, you compare two answers and say which one is better. That's cheaper for the annotator and it captures something that's hard to write down, this notion of taste. And it's what lets you push the model beyond what any single annotator would write, because the model can produce candidates and you only need humans to judge.

The last thing I'd say is that we try to keep that layer thin. We don't want to bake in too much personality or too many constraints, because our customers want to fine-tune, they want to deploy in their own context with their own tone. So for us the annotations are about making the model a good, controllable base, and leaving as much of the specialization as possible to the people who actually know their use case.

r001.rationale: The response describes human-written annotations and human comparisons as supervision, but does not identify machine-produced annotations as a possible source.

astra-6.text:
I think annotations are a way of specifying what you mean by following instructions. With pretraining, you get a model that has a lot of capabilities, but it’s trained to continue text. It’s not necessarily trained to answer your question in the way you expect.

So demonstrations and preference annotations help you bridge that gap. You show the model what a useful response looks like, or you tell it that one response is better than another. The quality and consistency of that signal matter a lot. If your annotators disagree about whether the model should be concise, ask a clarifying question, or give a detailed answer, then you’re giving it a somewhat contradictory objective.

And there’s a distinction between making the model more useful and making it look more useful. You can reward a very polished answer that is actually wrong. So the challenge is to make sure your annotations reward the behavior you really care about, rather than just a particular style of response.

r001.rationale: The response discusses demonstrations and preference annotations as supervision, but does not identify machine-produced annotations as a possible source.

sol-6.1.text:
I think annotations are useful for teaching a model how to interact, but they’re not where most of its capabilities come from. Those are largely acquired during pretraining. By the time you start instruction tuning, the model already knows a lot; what you’re doing is showing it how to use that knowledge in response to a request.

So the quality and consistency of the annotations matter a great deal. You want examples that make the intended behavior clear, and enough diversity that the model learns to follow instructions rather than imitate a particular format. It’s less about adding knowledge than about making the capabilities you already have accessible to the user.

r001.rationale: The response discusses annotations as instruction-tuning supervision, but does not identify them as machine-produced.
